traveler: Marie Adrienne Françoise de Noailles, Marquise de Lafayette
title: La femme Lafayette: the Hôtel de Noailles, the Common Pit, and the Prison She Chose
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hôtel de Noailles, the second daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested; the hôtel stood at nos. 219-223 rue Saint-Honoré and was demolished in 1830, so the pin is the block and not a doorway
stops.campa: In the Noailles townhouse on the rue Saint-Honoré a second daughter is born to Jean-Louis-Paul-François de Noailles, soon Duc d'Ayen, and Henriette-Anne-Louise d'Aguesseau. They name her Marie Adrienne Françoise. Five daughters and two sons will fill these rooms, and their mother teaches them herself: catechism, history, the household accounts, in a century that hands girls of this rank to convents and collects them again at fifteen. The first family of the French court is raising her. So is a woman who intends her to think.
suggested_refs: The site of the Hôtel de Noailles, nos. 219-223 rue Saint-Honoré, demolished 1830

stops.name: Hôtel de Noailles, the chapel and the contract
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the private chapel of her father's house Adrienne, fourteen and a half, marries Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, sixteen years and seven months old, an orphan with an enormous fortune and no conversation. The two houses arranged it. The French article that carries the date says he was seventeen; he was born on the sixth of September 1757, and the arithmetic does not hold. Neither of them chose this. Thirty-three years later she will die holding his hand, and the marriage will have been the only fixed point in a life the century tore apart four separate times.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier de La Fayette'
suggested_refs: The Histoire de Paris panel recording the marriage, misplaced at no. 211 rue Saint-Honoré

stops.name: Château de Versailles, presented at court
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; no date of presentation was confirmed in any source fetched, and the year is a placeholder
stops.campa: A Noailles bride is presented at Versailles as a matter of course, and the young Marquise de Lafayette enters the circle around Marie-Antoinette that her husband is already failing to charm. He dances badly, says little, and is laughed at. She is not laughed at. The court sees a devout, plain, exactly correct girl of the highest possible blood. It does not see that of the two of them she is the one whose nerve will hold after this room and everyone standing in it are gone.
sources: Lafayette-family biographical tradition; not verified in any source fetched
suggested_refs: The rituals of presentation at the court of Louis XVI

stops.name: Hôtel de Noailles, the first child
stops.date_confidence: attested by the en.wikipedia infobox; the French article dates the birth 1776, and this journey follows the English dates as the only pair corroborated elsewhere
stops.campa: Henriette du Motier de La Fayette is born, and Adrienne is sixteen. The two Wikipedias disagree about the year by twelve months and agree about the length of the child's life, twenty-two months, which is the figure everything else has to fit. She will have four children in seven years and bury one of them while their father is on another continent. The Noailles hôtel is where the convention of the period puts the birth; no source this journey could open names the room, and the child who is born in it has less than two years to live.
suggested_refs: The disputed 1775/1776 birth dates of Henriette du Motier de La Fayette

stops.name: Paris, Anastasie born as her father sails
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the day is tradition and no fetched source gives it
stops.campa: Lafayette has bought a ship and left the country against the express order of his king, to fight in a war on the far side of the Atlantic for a republic that has not yet won a battle. He lands in South Carolina in June. In Paris his wife, seventeen and pregnant with their second child, is left to hold the position with his creditors, his king, and her own furious father. Anastasie Louise Pauline is born in the summer of the same year. The child's father is on the Delaware, being shot through the leg at Brandywine, and will not see her for two years.
sources: fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, 'Adrienne de La Fayette'
en.wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'
suggested_refs: Lafayette's unauthorized 1777 departure and the royal order forbidding it

stops.name: Paris, the death of Henriette
stops.date_confidence: attested by the en.wikipedia infobox; the French article dates the death 1778
stops.campa: The first child dies at twenty-two months. Her father is in America and will not return until February 1779, so the news crosses the ocean at the speed of a sailing packet and reaches him months late, in a camp, in a language he is still learning. Adrienne buries the child alone. Nothing in the record says what she wrote to him about it. This is the first of the four times she will be left to carry the household through a catastrophe he is not present for, and the only one that has no politics in it at all.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'
suggested_refs: The transatlantic mail delays of the American war

stops.name: Château de Chavaniac, the Auvergne household
stops.date_confidence: tradition; universal in Lafayette biography and confirmed by nothing fetched this session, and the date is a placeholder inside the American years
stops.campa: Biography puts her for long stretches at her husband's ancestral house in the Haute-Loire, high volcanic country three hundred miles from the court, under the eye of his aunt Madame de Chavaniac, raising the children among people who speak Occitan. Nothing fetched for this journey confirms a single one of those months. The tradition is repeated everywhere and sourced nowhere, and it is recorded here as tradition, because the alternative is to invent a Paris that the record does not supply either.
sources: Lafayette-family biographical tradition; not verified in any source fetched
suggested_refs: The Château de Chavaniac, Lafayette's birthplace and family seat in the Haute-Loire

stops.name: Hôtel de Noailles, the Queen at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Lafayette comes home from America a hero of two continents, briefly under house arrest for having gone at all, and the punishment lasts about a week. Marie-Antoinette comes to the Hôtel de Noailles in person to see the wife of the man who fought at Brandywine. The girl who was laughed at for her husband's silence is now the woman the Queen calls on. Adrienne is nineteen. She has buried a daughter and raised two children through the whole of it, and the court has decided, retroactively, that this was romantic.
suggested_refs: The 1779 return of Lafayette and the reception at the Hôtel de Noailles

stops.name: Paris, a son named for a foreign general
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Paris address of the birth is not confirmed in any source fetched
stops.campa: The boy is christened Georges Washington Louis Gilbert du Motier de La Fayette, and the name is a political act performed on an infant: a French marquis's heir carrying the name of a rebel commander whose country has no king. He will be hidden at fourteen, shipped to America at fifteen to live in the President's own house, and buried in 1849 having outlived the Revolution, the Empire, the Restoration, and both his parents. His mother chose the name while his father was in Paris drumming up a fleet for Rochambeau.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Lafayette and Washington on the naming of the boy

stops.name: Paris, the last child
stops.date_confidence: attested; the earlier dossier gave 24 September, which the source does not support, and the Paris address is convention
stops.campa: Marie-Antoinette-Virginie is born, named for the Queen and for the American state where her father commanded. Popular accounts credit the second name to a suggestion from Thomas Jefferson; Jefferson does not reach France until August 1784, two years after this birth, and the story is dropped here. Virginie will follow her mother into an Austrian fortress at thirteen and outlive her by forty-two years. Almost every surviving word of Adrienne's reaches the world through the biography Virginie writes.
suggested_refs: Virginie de Lasteyrie, Vie de Madame de Lafayette, 2nd ed. 1869

segments.name: The House on the Rue de Bourbon

stops.name: Rue de Bourbon, a house of their own
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the pin is the corner of the rue de Lille and the rue de Bourgogne, where the French sources place the house at no. 81
stops.campa: The family leaves the Noailles compound for the Hôtel de La Fayette on the rue de Bourbon, on the Left Bank, almost at the corner of the rue de Bourgogne. For the first time Adrienne runs her own house rather than a wing of her father's. It becomes the address where American visitors are received and where Lafayette's abolition schemes and constitutional drafts are argued over. Nine years from now the commander of the National Guard will be living here on the day the monarchy he is sworn to protect stops existing.
suggested_refs: No. 81 rue de Lille, formerly the Hôtel de La Fayette on the rue de Bourbon

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the Fête de la Fédération
stops.date_confidence: the ceremony is attested; her presence at it is tradition and is confirmed by no source fetched
stops.campa: A year to the day after the Bastille, an enormous crowd fills the Champ de Mars and Lafayette, commanding the National Guard, administers the civic oath before the king. It is the last hour in which the Revolution and the monarchy can be photographed standing in the same frame. In Spain that same July a boy named José de San Martín is entered as a cadet in the Regiment of Murcia. Whether Adrienne is in the stands is not recorded anywhere reachable, and her absence from the record here is itself the pattern.
sources: Revolutionary-era biographical tradition; her attendance not verified
suggested_refs: The Fête de la Fédération, 14 July 1790

stops.name: Tuileries Palace, the tenth of August
stops.date_confidence: the storming is attested; this stop marks the event that ends her husband's position, not a movement of hers
stops.campa: The palace is stormed, the Swiss Guard is killed on the staircases, and the constitutional monarchy Lafayette spent three years trying to build ends in an afternoon. He is with the Army of the North and has already tried, twice, to turn his troops on the Jacobin clubs. The Assembly will vote him a traitor within days. The same courtyards will hold Napoleon's divorce in 1809 and the birth of the King of Rome in 1811. For the woman on the rue de Bourbon, the tenth of August is the day her name becomes a charge.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'
suggested_refs: The storming of the Tuileries, 10 August 1792

stops.name: Paris, the husband taken by the Austrians
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pin is the canonical Paris coordinate this atlas shares, since the capture itself happens on the Austrian Netherlands frontier
stops.campa: Lafayette rides out of France rather than be arrested and is taken by Austrian troops at the frontier, beginning five years of imprisonment at Wesel, then Magdeburg, then the Moravian fortress of Olmütz. He has escaped the Jacobins by handing himself to the enemy of the Republic, which makes him a traitor in both directions and his family hostages in Paris. Georges, twelve, goes into hiding in September. Adrienne stays where she is, under a name that is now, in the phrase her biographer will use, a death warrant in itself.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'
suggested_refs: The Austrian and Prussian prisons of Lafayette, 1792-1797

stops.name: Château de Chavaniac, the émigré's wife
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the raw wikitext of both the French and English articles was checked and neither mentions Chavaniac, 1792, or the Auvergne, so the earlier attested tag was withdrawn
stops.campa: The tradition holds that she withdraws with the children to her husband's country house, five hundred miles from the tribunals, and becomes the most conspicuous woman in a poor department: the wife of a declared traitor, living in the family château, watched by a local committee that reports to Paris. The tradition may be right. It is carried by every biography and by no article this journey could open, and the honest form of the sentence is that the record for these two years is missing.
sources: Lafayette-family biographical tradition; explicitly not supported by the articles cited for it in the earlier dossier
suggested_refs: Departmental surveillance records of the Haute-Loire, 1792-1794

stops.name: Château de Chavaniac, the Law of Suspects
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the earlier dossier dated this house arrest 1792-1793, which is impossible, since the Law of Suspects was decreed on 17 September 1793
stops.campa: The Convention decrees that anyone who by conduct, associations, talk, or writing has shown himself a partisan of tyranny is a suspect, and orders the committees to arrest them. The relatives of émigrés are named in the text. Adrienne is, by the letter of the decree, twice condemned in advance: a Noailles and a Lafayette. She is placed under house arrest and begins the correspondence that will be her whole method for the next four years, petition after petition to men who can have her killed for writing.
sources: Lafayette-family biographical tradition for the arrest itself
suggested_refs: The text of the Law of Suspects, 17 September 1793

stops.name: Brioude, the local gaol
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; the pin is the town centre and no building is identified in any source fetched
stops.campa: Some accounts move her from house arrest to a prison in the small Allier-valley town, a stage on the way north. The stop is here because the tradition is old and consistent, and it is flagged because nothing this journey could reach names the building, the date, or the order that sent her. The Terror in the departments kept worse records than the Terror in Paris, and the wife of the most famous traitor in France passes through this stretch of it almost invisibly.
suggested_refs: Revolutionary prison registers of the Haute-Loire, at Brioude and Le Puy

stops.name: Le Puy-en-Velay, the departmental prison
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; the pin is the town centre, and both the building and the dates are gaps
stops.campa: The prefecture town under its volcanic needles holds the departmental prison, and tradition puts her in it before the transfer to Paris. Her children are elsewhere. Her husband is in a Prussian casemate. Her mother, grandmother, and sister are alive in Paris and will be dead within six months. From here the machinery that has been consuming the French nobility by category rather than by act reaches down into the Auvergne and calls her up to the capital, where the category has a courtroom.
suggested_refs: The revolutionary prisons of Le Puy-en-Velay

stops.name: Paris, the prison no source will name
stops.date_confidence: the imprisonment is certain and its address is an open gap; popular accounts name the Collège du Plessis, others La Force, and no source fetched names any prison at all
stops.campa: She is held in Paris through the worst weeks of the Terror, and the record loses the address. What survives is the method. Every petition she submits to the revolutionary administration opens with the same two words, her husband's proscribed name written out in her own hand at the head of the page, when concealment was available and would have been sensible. Somewhere in this same prison system Francisco de Miranda, acquitted once by the Tribunal and rearrested, is writing petitions of his own.
stops.quote_source: The formula heading every petition Adrienne de Lafayette submitted to the revolutionary administration during the Terror, in M. MacDermot Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), pp. 2 and 202
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), pp. 2, 202, 246, 330, 331
miranda.journey.json (La Force and the Revolutionary Tribunal)
suggested_refs: The prison registers of Paris, an XII, for the detention of the citoyenne Lafayette

stops.name: Place du Trône-Renversé, the twenty-second of July
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Three generations of Noailles women go up in one batch: Catherine de Cossé-Brissac, Duchesse de Noailles, her daughter-in-law Henriette d'Aguesseau, Duchesse d'Ayen, and Henriette's daughter Anne, Vicomtesse de Noailles. The grandmother, the mother, and the sister. Five days later Robespierre falls and the guillotine stops. Adrienne is in a cell somewhere in the same city and learns of it there. Her mother had been arrested at the Hôtel de Noailles in May, in the house where Adrienne was born and married.
suggested_refs: The scaffold of the Place du Trône-Renversé, June and July 1794

stops.name: Cimetière de Picpus, the common pit
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pit received the dead of the Place du Trône-Renversé between 14 June and 27 July 1794
stops.campa: The bodies from the Place du Trône-Renversé are carted to a walled garden in the faubourg Saint-Antoine and tipped into two quarry pits, one thousand three hundred and six of them in six weeks, nobles and nuns and locksmiths together. The three Noailles women are in there, unmarked and unsorted. When the killing stops the families of the dead buy the ground. Adrienne will be buried at the edge of this pit thirteen years from now, and her husband beside her forty years from now, under American soil.
suggested_refs: The two mass graves of the Cimetière de Picpus and the list of the 1,306

stops.name: Paris, Elizabeth Monroe at the prison door
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the whole episode rests on a section of the English Wikipedia article that carries an Unreferenced banner, which names no prison and cites nothing, and which dates it 1795 while the same dossier's other lens dates it 1794
stops.campa: The story runs like this. The wife of the American minister to France drives to the prison in the legation carriage, asks to see the citoyenne Lafayette, weeps with her in front of the guards, and announces loudly on leaving that she will return tomorrow. The Committee reads the message: the United States is watching this one. The sentence is reversed. It is the best-known thing anyone says about Adrienne de Lafayette and it is carried by a single unreferenced paragraph, which is exactly how such stories are usually carried.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Adrienne de La Fayette' (section flagged Unreferenced)
suggested_refs: The despatches of James Monroe as United States minister to France, 1794-1796

stops.name: Paris, released
stops.date_confidence: the standard biographical date; not confirmed in any article fetched, and the release circumstances are tradition
stops.campa: She walks out into a Paris that has stopped executing people and has not stopped hating the name she signed her petitions with. Her mother, grandmother, and sister are in a pit across the city. Her husband is in Moravia and no one will tell her where exactly. Her son is fifteen and hunted. Her two daughters are alive. She has, at thirty-five, no money, no house, and no protection except a foreign legation, and she spends the next nine months converting that into a passport.
suggested_refs: The release of noble prisoners in Paris after 9 Thermidor

stops.name: Le Havre, the son shipped west
stops.date_confidence: the departure for the United States in April 1795 is attested; the port is tradition and is not confirmed, and her presence at the quay is unverified
stops.campa: Georges Washington de La Fayette, fifteen, is put on a ship for America with his tutor Félix Frestel and a letter to the President whose name he carries. His mother is arranging her own journey in the opposite direction, toward the fortress where his father is. She is dividing the family deliberately: the heir out of reach of the Republic, the daughters with her into an imperial prison. Every biography since has called this maternal devotion. It is closer to a deployment.
suggested_refs: Frestel's account of the crossing and the reception by Washington

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the boy in the President's house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the boy divides his American time between the presidential residence in Philadelphia and Mount Vernon
stops.campa: The son lives as George Washington's guest, at the presidential residence in Philadelphia and on the Potomac plantation, for three years. The President is cautious about it in public, since the boy's father is a diplomatic problem with three governments, and unreserved about it in private. It is the only debt from the American war anyone in this family is able to collect. Georges will sail home in 1798 to a mother who has spent the intervening years in an Austrian cell by choice.
suggested_refs: Washington's correspondence concerning young Lafayette, 1795-1797

stops.name: Hofburg, Vienna, the audience with Francis II
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the article cited for this in the earlier dossier contains no mention of Vienna, Francis II, or a passport, and the Hofburg as the room is an assumption, though her own letter of February 1796 refers to leaving the Emperor's presence
stops.campa: Travelling on an American passport issued in the name of a Mrs Motier, she reaches Vienna and asks the Holy Roman Emperor for permission to be imprisoned. He grants it, on one condition she does not yet know about. No article this journey could open names the audience; her own letter from Olmütz five months later speaks of what she had imagined on leaving Your Majesty's presence, which is the closest thing to a witness the record provides, and it is her.
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 282, for her own reference to the audience
suggested_refs: Austrian state chancellery records of audiences granted by Francis II, 1795

stops.name: Olmütz, the gate closes behind her
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pin is the city, since which building of the fortress held them is a gap
stops.campa: Adrienne arrives at the Moravian fortress with Anastasie, eighteen, and Virginie, thirteen, and the three of them are locked in with Lafayette. It is damp, unheated, and unventilated; the daughters share one cell and their parents another. She has come from a French prison to an Austrian one on her own initiative and she is the only person in the building who is there voluntarily. Fifty-five years later Mikhail Bakunin will be tried in this same fortress town and sentenced to death twice.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Olomouc and the cells of the state prisoners

stops.name: Olmütz, the letter to the Emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is printed in Crawford (1907) at p. 282, not p. 281 as the earlier dossier had it, the folios in that book being printed at the foot of the page
stops.campa: Four months in, her health failing, she writes to Francis II. The letter thanks him first, in the full formula, for the permission to be a prisoner. It refuses to describe her husband's condition, which is worse than she had been led to expect, and says so in a subordinate clause. Then it asks for a few days in Vienna to see doctors, leaving her daughters with their father. Every sentence is correct and every sentence is a bill being presented. She is thirty-six and has not been outdoors in months.
stops.quote: Sire: Had I sooner been given leave to write, I should long since have offered my grateful thanks to Your Imperial Majesty for having permitted us to share the captivity of one so dear. To these thanks, Sire, I shall add no details of M. de Lafayette's condition, however different it may be from what I imagined on leaving Your Majesty's presence; to my great regret I shall only speak of myself. My health, impaired by sufferings and misfortunes, my duty towards those who are still left to me in this world constrains me to solicit permission to go for some days to Vienna, leaving my daughters with their father, in order to consult doctors on my state.
stops.quote_source: Mme de Lafayette to the Emperor Francis II, Olmütz, 6 February 1796, in M. MacDermot Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (New York: James Pott & Co., 1907), p. 282
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 282, verified against the Internet Archive page images
suggested_refs: The Olmütz letters of Mme de Lafayette, in Crawford (1907)

stops.name: Olmütz, the answer to the Commandant
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Emperor's answer comes back through the fortress commander two months later. She may leave to see her doctors, and she may never come back. The permission and the sentence are the same sentence. She refuses in four lines, in the third person, with the formality of a woman declining an invitation, and stays in the cell. Her health does not recover; the illness she is refusing to treat is the one that kills her eleven years later. This is the decision the rest of her reputation rests on, and it is two paragraphs long.
stops.quote: The Commander of Olmutz having declared to me that on my request to go for a week to Vienna in order to consult the doctors, his Imperial Majesty does not permit me, under any pretense whatever, to go to Vienna, and only allows me to leave this prison on condition never to enter it again, I have the honour here to renew my answer. It was my duty towards my family and friends to try and obtain the advice necessary for my health, but they well know that I cannot accept the conditions offered to me.
stops.quote_source: Mme de Lafayette to the Commander of Olmütz, 4 April 1796, in Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 282
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 282
suggested_refs: The imperial order of April 1796 conditioning her medical leave on permanent exclusion

stops.name: Olmütz, the letter to Bollmann
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Justus Erich Bollmann, a German physician, and Francis Kinloch Huger, a South Carolinian whose father had housed Lafayette on his first night in America, tried to break him out of Austrian custody in 1794 and were imprisoned for it. From inside the cell their failure produced, Adrienne writes to thank Bollmann. The letter is short and says only that she is at last permitted to write and that gratitude is the first thing she wants on paper. Her correspondence is her only remaining instrument and she keeps it in perfect order.
stops.quote: I am at last enabled to write to you, and to express to you all the sentiments with which we are so deeply affected. The first wish of my heart is to assure you of our gratitude.
stops.quote_source: Mme de Lafayette to Dr Justus Erich Bollmann, Olmütz, 22 May 1796, in Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 333
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 333
suggested_refs: The Bollmann and Huger escape attempt of November 1794

stops.name: Olmütz, the life of her mother
stops.date_confidence: the memoir is attested as written during the Olmütz captivity; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: In the cell she writes a life of her mother, the Duchesse d'Ayen, in the first person, in ink she has to argue for. The subject was beheaded two years earlier and thrown into a pit her daughter has never seen. The book reconstructs the winter of 1793, her mother and her sister moving around a hunted Paris trying to learn what had become of Lafayette, and looking, above all, for the sacraments. The sentence that carries the whole thing is a single line of theology written by a prisoner about a woman the state destroyed.
stops.quote: Let us adore the will of God and the means he employs for the sanctification of his elect.
stops.quote_source: Adrienne de Lafayette, Life of the Duchesse d'Ayen, written at Olmütz, in Life of Madame de Lafayette, preceded by the Life of the Duchesse d'Ayen, trans. Louis de Lasteyrie (London: Barthes and Lowell, 1872), p. 106
sources: Life of Madame de Lafayette, preceded by the Life of the Duchesse d'Ayen (1872), p. 106, verified in the Internet Archive scan
suggested_refs: Adrienne de Lafayette's Vie de la Duchesse d'Ayen, composed in captivity

stops.name: Olmütz, what the daughter saw
stops.date_confidence: the account is attested; the month is a placeholder within the captivity
stops.campa: Virginie, writing long afterwards, remembers a mother who was cheerful in the cell, glad of her husband's company, taking pleasure in the quiet, and remembers too that this cheerfulness fooled her children into worrying less than they should have. The illness advanced under it. The composure that makes the legend is the same composure that hid the symptoms from the only three people in a position to see them, and the daughter who writes the sentence is still, decades on, reproaching herself for having believed it.
stops.quote: Seeing her always serene, always enjoying my father's company and the consolations she had brought with her, we were all less anxious than we ought to have been. This explains how, save in the beginning of the illness, she found pleasure in our quiet life.
stops.quote_source: Virginie de Lafayette, Mme de Lasteyrie, on the Olmütz captivity, in Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 283
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 283
suggested_refs: Virginie de Lasteyrie's recollections of the Olmütz cells

stops.name: Olmütz, the doors open
stops.date_confidence: 19 September 1797 is the date in most Lafayette scholarship; the earlier dossier split between 18 and 19 September, tied the release to the Treaty of Campo Formio, which was not signed until 17 October, and the American Battlefield Trust dates the release to 1799, a conflict left open
stops.campa: Bonaparte, having beaten Austria into the preliminaries of Leoben in April, presses Vienna on the point, and the family walks out of the fortress after almost two years. The treaty the story is usually attached to, Campo Formio, is signed a month after they are already free, so it cannot be the instrument, and one American reference work puts the release two years later still. Adrienne leaves the building unable to walk unaided. Napoleon has just opened a door that the woman on the other side of it will spend the rest of her life declining to thank him for.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'
American Battlefield Trust, 'Marquis de Lafayette' (which dates the release 1799)
suggested_refs: The Preliminaries of Leoben, 18 April 1797, and the Austrian release of the Olmütz prisoners

stops.name: Hamburg, the merchant who paid
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Parish credit; the earlier dossier made Hamburg the family's residence, which the German source does not support
stops.campa: Released and barred from France, the family has no money at all. John Parish, a Hamburg merchant, extends the credit that rents them a roof. Hamburg is where the account is, not where they live, and the distinction matters because the standard account of these years puts them in the city itself. The Lafayettes at this point are stateless: unwelcome in the Republic, unwelcome in the emigration, and in debt to a banker in a free Hanseatic port who has decided that a famous ruin is worth backing.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg house of John Parish and its credit to the Lafayette family

stops.name: Lehmkuhlen, the rented manor
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1797; the earlier dossier gave coordinates matching neither Lehmkuhlen nor Wittmoldt and kept the family here until 1799 rather than 1798
stops.campa: They take a manor house in Danish Holstein, north of the Elbe and outside every jurisdiction that wants them. Adrienne is recovering from two years of confinement and is not recovering well; the family's account is that she never does. Georges comes back from America in 1798 and the family is complete for the first time since 1792, in a rented Baltic farmhouse, on borrowed money, under a flag none of them had heard of ten years earlier. They stay less than a year, and the year is the calmest the four of them will ever have together.
suggested_refs: Gut Lehmkuhlen, near Plön, Holstein

stops.name: Wittmoldt, the aunt down the road
stops.date_confidence: attested that Mme de Tessé lived at Wittmoldt from 1797; the earlier dossier wrongly made the Lehmkuhlen estate hers, and the English article compounds the confusion by calling Mme de Montagu an aunt when she was Adrienne's sister
stops.campa: Adrienne's aunt, Adrienne Catherine de Noailles, Comtesse de Tessé, has bought an estate a few miles off and is running a small French colony of survivors in the Holstein lake country. Her sister Pauline, Marquise de Montagu, is nearby too. What assembles here is what is left of the Noailles, the women who were not in Paris in July 1794. They farm Danish land, they compare lists of the dead, and they wait for a government in France willing to let them come home.
suggested_refs: Gut Wittmoldt and the Noailles emigration in Holstein

stops.name: Vianen, the Dutch stage
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the Dutch stage of the exile is not confirmed in any source fetched, and the earlier dossier's attribution of the property to Mme de Tessé is unsupported, since she remained at Wittmoldt until 1804
stops.campa: The exile moves south into the Batavian Republic, closer to the French border, which is the point. From Holland Adrienne works the intermediaries: former deputies, bankers, anyone with access to the Directory and later to the Consulate. Her husband will not petition, on principle, having been declared a traitor by an assembly he considers illegitimate. She has no such difficulty. She spent 1794 signing her name as the traitor's wife, and the practice of asking hostile governments for things is by now a trade she has mastered.
suggested_refs: The Batavian Republic and the French émigré return negotiations, 1798-1800

stops.name: Paris, the border opens
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the return follows the coup of 18 Brumaire, and no re-entry point or date was confirmed
stops.campa: After Brumaire the new First Consul lets them come back. Lafayette returns to a country he will spend the next thirty-four years opposing, refusing the Senate, refusing the Legion of Honour, voting against the Empire in a plebiscite where the negative votes are counted in the low thousands. Adrienne returns to a city with her family in a pit at Picpus and her own house gone. She is forty, and she begins, immediately, the work of getting the property back.
suggested_refs: The Consulate's amnesties and the return of the émigrés, 1800-1802

segments.name: La Grange and the Pit at Picpus

stops.name: Château de La Grange-Bléneau, the house she recovers
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1802 as the start of Lafayette's residence; the earlier dossier said she bought the estate with her own money in 1800, where the French source has it coming through her family's holdings
stops.campa: The moated brick château in the Brie comes to her through the Noailles inheritance and passes from her to her husband, who will live in it until he dies in 1834. It becomes the address of the international liberal opposition: Jefferson's correspondents, Italian carbonari, Greek and Polish exiles, and eventually Fenimore Cooper, all making the day's ride from Paris. Adrienne rebuilds the family's finances from these fields. The men who visit come to see the hero of two worlds, and the estate they walk through is hers.
suggested_refs: The Château de La Grange-Bléneau, Courpalay, and the Lafayette archive kept there

stops.name: 24 rue d'Anjou, the last illness
stops.date_confidence: the address and the death are attested; the attribution of the illness to the Olmütz confinement is tradition and rests on no medical or primary source
stops.campa: She is brought to a house on the rue d'Anjou and does not leave it. The family has always said Olmütz killed her, ten years late, and no medical record exists to test the claim. Lafayette sits with her through the whole of it. He is a man who has been imprisoned by three governments, shot at on two continents, and declared a traitor twice, and the letter he writes afterwards to La Tour Maubourg makes plain that this fortnight in a Paris bedroom is the thing that broke him.
stops.quote_source: Crawford's narrative of the deathbed, in Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 318; the same words recur inside Lafayette's own letter to M. de La Tour Maubourg of January 1808 at p. 328
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), pp. 318 and 328
suggested_refs: Lafayette's letter to M. de La Tour Maubourg, January 1808

stops.name: 24 rue d'Anjou, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested by the French article, which gives the street address; the English article's 25 December and its placing of the death in Auvergne both sit inside a section flagged Unreferenced and are treated here as error rather than as a live dispute
stops.campa: She dies on Christmas Eve, forty-eight years old. Her husband's account gives the order of it: she speaks first, then her right hand goes still on his and keeps pressing, and the pressure means what the words meant. Tradition holds that the phrase was her wedding vow, spoken at fourteen in the chapel of her father's house, returned at the end; nothing in the sources supports that, and it has been repeated for two centuries because it is the shape the life already has.
stops.quote: What a blessing! how happy I am to be yours!
stops.quote_source: Adrienne de Lafayette's last words, in Lafayette's letter to M. de La Tour Maubourg, January 1808, printed in Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 328
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), p. 328
suggested_refs: The house at 24 rue d'Anjou, Paris 8e

stops.name: Cimetière de Picpus, buried at the edge of the pit
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Picpus is attested and the day is not established in any source fetched; that she chose the ground to lie near her mother, grandmother, and sister is family tradition
stops.campa: She is buried in the walled garden in the faubourg Saint-Antoine, a few yards from the quarry pit that holds her mother, her grandmother, and her sister, thirteen years after the carts came. The families of the guillotined bought this ground precisely so that the anonymous dead could be visited by somebody. There is no statue of Adrienne de Lafayette anywhere in France or America, no street named for her, no square; the monuments and the place-names all belong to her husband. There is this plot, and the fact that she chose it herself.
stops.quote: She was a model of heroism. She was one of the few whose unsullied reputation received new lustre from the misfortunes of the Revolution.
stops.quote_source: Louis-Philippe, Comte de Ségur, quoted in Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), Preface, p. vii
sources: Crawford, Madame de Lafayette and Her Family (1907), Preface, p. vii
suggested_refs: The Lafayette plot at the Cimetière de Picpus, beside the common grave

stops.name: Cimetière de Picpus, the husband and the flag
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Lafayette dies in 1834 and is buried beside her under soil he had shipped home from Bunker Hill, so that the two graves lie in French ground and American earth at once. An American flag has flown over the plot ever since, renewed each Fourth of July by the Daughters of the American Revolution with the Society of the Cincinnati and the embassy. It is the only continuous commemoration attached to this place, and it honours him. Her name is on the stone beside his, and the pit is a few yards away.
suggested_refs: The annual Fourth of July ceremony at the Lafayette grave, Picpus
